Our findings establish Ctf4 not merely as a structural scaffold, but as a central chaperone at the replication fork that actively governs symmetric partitioning of parental histones, thereby ensuring the fidelity of epigenetic memory through successive cell divisions.

articles_hidden.title: Interploidy massively increases meiotic crossovers in pericentromeric recombination deserts
articles_hidden.authors: Loeiz Maillet, Virginie Huteau, Noémie Guiziou, Olivier Coriton, Maryse Taburel-Lodé, Ewen Le Seyec, Matthieu Falque, Olivier Martin, Annaliese S. Mason, Marie Devers, Franz Boideau, Anne-Marie Chèvre, Mathieu Rousseau-Gueutin
articles_hidden.abstract: Meiotic recombination reshuffles genetic diversity through reciprocal DNA exchanges between chromosomes known as crossovers. In most eukaryotes, crossovers are highly constrained in both frequency and distribution, leaving large genomic regions with little or no recombination. A notable exception is the Brassica AAC allotriploid hybrid obtained from a cross between allotetraploid Brassica napus (AACC) and diploid Brassica rapa (AA), which exhibits elevated recombination and crossover formation near centromeres. Here, we generated a CCA allotriploid hybrid from a cross between B. napus and Brassica oleracea (CC), and subsequently produced AAC allotriploids by crossing the CCA hybrid with B. rapa . Both CCA and AAC allotriploids exhibit similar meiotic deregulation, demonstrating that this phenomenon is not restricted to AAC hybrids. Both systems displayed a marked increase in crossover frequency within normally low-recombining chromosome regions, reaching 9.4-fold in AAC and 13.4-fold in CCA allotriploids. Alternating CCA and AAC allotriploids efficiently reshuffled both B. napus subgenomes within only two generations. Using genetic mapping and cytogenetics, we further identified homoeologous exchanges. Remarkably, crossovers occurring on chromosomes involved in homoeologous associations exhibited a more pronounced redistribution toward nonrecombining regions than those on homologously paired chromosomes. Moreover, the frequency of homoeologous associations varied with the diploid progenitor genotype, indicating that genetic factors controlling homoeologous recombination already exist in Brassica diploids. Altogether, our results identify allotriploidy as a simple and powerful strategy to unlock recombination deserts, which harbor 21% of total resistance gene analogs, and provide insights into its potential role in allopolyploid evolution, adaptation, and speciation.

articles_hidden.title: The Yersinia pestis effector YopM binds the human pyrin death domain to inhibit inflammasome activation and effector-triggered immunity
articles_hidden.authors: Bethany W. Mwaura, Adam R. Simard, Kate M. Brown, Morgan L. Pettis, Ao Liu, Dean R. Madden, James B. Bliska
articles_hidden.abstract: Bacteria in the genus Yersinia use type III secretion to inject several effectors into phagocytes to disrupt signaling. Two effectors disrupt host signaling by inactivation of RhoA, triggering pyrin inflammasome assembly in infected phagocytes and protective immunity. A third protein, YopM, counteracts effector-triggered immunity by binding to and inactivating pyrin. Prior evidence suggested that gain of function codon changes in the pyrin gene MEFV that cause Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) and provide resistance to Yersinia pestis were selected to evade YopM binding. YopM was shown to bind an N-terminal region of human pyrin, which includes the eponymous pyrin domain (PYD), however, the interaction mechanism was undefined. Using bacterial two-hybrid assay, protein biochemistry, and X-ray crystallography, we determined that YopM binds to the PYD, which has few validated FMF amino acid variants. We show that YopM binds PYD R42, a “Site 2” amino acid important for positive and negative regulation of pyrin and that binding to the R42W variant is reduced. YopM amino acid change variants defective for PYD binding failed to inhibit the pyrin inflammasome in human monocytes infected with Yersinia . In addition, PYD binding was dispensable for YopM to inhibit the inflammasome in murine macrophages, suggesting this effector uses a distinct mechanism to target mouse pyrin. These results define that Y. pestis YopM binds to human PYD to promote pathogenesis, and because Site 2 variants that evade YopM binding have low gain of function inflammasome activity, these data may explain why most validated FMF codon changes are in other domains of pyrin.

articles_hidden.title: Glycosaminoglycans in the structures of Aβ 42 amyloid fibrils purified from mouse brains
articles_hidden.authors: Dev Thacker, Alexander I. P. Taylor, Martin Wilkinson, Felecia Sutton, Jonathan M. Machin, Nayab Fatima, René A. W. Frank, Jessica C. F. Kwok, Neil A. Ranson, Sheena E. Radford
articles_hidden.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has revealed the structures of the ordered cores of amyloid fibrils assembled in vitro and isolated from diseased tissue. Many of the ex vivo amyloid structures contain low-resolution density adjacent to the protein core, often attributed to nonproteinaceous ligands, yet their identity has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize such density in distinct polymorphs of Aβ fibrils purified from the brains of homozygous App NL-F and App NL-G-F knock-in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease. In App NL-G-F fibrils, which are built from the Arctic Aβ variant (E22G), we use immunogold labeling, immunofluorescence microscopy, and cryo-EM to identify the density as the glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate. These GAGs bind to an exposed positively charged patch on the Aβ 42 fibril surface, forming an intimate peptide-GAG copolymer through stacking interactions with the amyloid core. In App NL-F fibrils the predominant polymorph (~ 85% of particles) is glycan-free, with the relevant side chains identified in the App NL-G-F fibrils being buried within the App NL-F fibril core. Formation of the glycan-binding site in a rare polymorph hence involves conformational rearrangement to create the required binding surface. Our findings reveal a structural basis for GAG incorporation into brain-derived amyloid fibrils and highlight amyloid-associated ligands as potential therapeutic targets in protein aggregation disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Topological validation of generated scientific images
articles_hidden.authors: Asim K. Dey, Jaidev Goel, Snigdhansu Chatterjee, Yulia R. Gel, H. Vincent Poor
articles_hidden.abstract: Synthetic data have become an indispensable tool for validation, standards development, and product design across a broad range of scientific and engineering disciplines. One of the earliest examples arose in energy systems, where security and confidentiality constraints motivated the development of synthetic power grids and, in turn, novel topological and geometric approaches for evaluating their fidelity. Today, synthetic scientific imagery has emerged as a new critical tool in a variety of applications, ranging from autonomous driving, robotics, and Internet-of-Things technologies to in silico trials, digital twins, and remote sensing of environment. Yet the rigorous assessment of such synthetic images and quantification of their associated uncertainties remains a fundamental challenge. Building on the recent advances in the topological and geometric validation of synthetic power grids, we develop a systematic framework for comparing image data through the persistence of their multiscale shape patterns using the statistical formalism of survival analysis. While the tools of persistent homology and statistical survival analysis are both mature methodologies, they have so far developed largely in isolation. Unlike more traditional comparison methods such as pixel-level similarity or distributional summaries that often fail to capture the complex, multiscale structural characteristics of modern scientific imagery, our approach shows the capability to systematically assess the mismatch between different images at all scales simultaneously, while characterizing the associated uncertainty. The resulting synergistic methodology establishes a broadly applicable statistical topological framework for validating synthetic scientific imagery and, more generally, complex synthetic data products.

articles_hidden.title: Phase coding supports neuronal replication and enables combinatorial problem solving
articles_hidden.authors: Hamza Giaffar, Márton Csillag, Zoltan Nadasdy, Dániel Czégel, Eörs Szathmáry
articles_hidden.abstract: Darwinian neurodynamics posits that the brain searches large solution spaces through iterated cycles of variation and selection on competing neural representations. Testing this hypothesis requires a biologically plausible neural replicator: a mechanism that copies spatiotemporal signals faithfully enough to cumulatively improve good solutions, yet loosely enough to allow exploration. We show that phase-coded spike patterns constitute such a replicator. Spike timing referenced to a local field oscillation is compressed into a transferable spike train and reconstructed by coincidence with the receiver’s own field, without synaptic plasticity or a shared code key. As replication noise rises, the system crosses two thresholds. Below the first, faithful copying sustains patterns as dynamic memory. Between the two thresholds, pattern populations evolve. On two hard combinatorial benchmarks, the traveling salesman problem and NK fitness landscapes, neural replication remains competitive with standard search methods at a matched evaluation budget. Beyond the second, an Eigen-like error threshold, inherited information collapses. The network architecture tunes the exploration-exploitation balance: high-degree lattices, where local competition is stronger, exploit smooth landscapes, while low-degree lattices, where weaker competition preserves diversity, search more broadly on rugged landscapes. The framework predicts phase-locked information transfer and phylogenetic structure in replay, as well as a selective loss of combinatorial problem solving beyond the error threshold. These results indicate that a single neurobiological substrate can support memory, variation, and selection, and point to evolutionary dynamics as a candidate computational principle for cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Wnts are endothelial cell–derived PKD1/PKD2-dependent autocrine/paracrine vasodilators
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich C. Mbiakop, Charles E. MacKay, Alejandro Mata-Daboin, Tessa A. C. Garrud, Roberto Braz Pontes, M. Dennis Leo, Jonathan H. Jaggar
articles_hidden.abstract: Wingless/Int-1 (Wnts) are secreted glycoproteins and canonical Frizzled receptor ligands. Recent evidence indicates that some Wnts can also bind to polycystin 1 (PKD1), a large transmembrane protein which can couple to polycystin 2 (PKD2) to form a nonselective cation channel. The functional significance of PKD1, PKD2, and Wnt-mediated PKD1 signaling in native cell types is poorly understood. Here, we tested the hypothesis that Wnts regulate arterial contractility, investigated the signaling mechanisms and cell types involved, and examined the cellular source of vasoactive Wnts. Our data show that Wnt9b and Wnt5a are endothelial cell (EC)-dependent vasodilators. Wnt9b stimulates vasodilation via EC PKD1/PKD2, whereas Wnt5a acts via both EC PKD1/PKD2 and Frizzled receptors. Wnts stimulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase and small conductance Ca 2+ -activated K + channels in ECs to produce vasodilation. Wnt9b and Wnt5a are present in plasma and intravenous infusion of Wnt9b stimulates an EC PKD1-dependent reduction in systemic blood pressure. Intravascular flow activates angiotensin II type 1 receptors which, through G q/11 and Porcupine signaling, stimulate ECs to secrete Wnt9b and Wnt5a. Wnts which are secreted by ECs in response to flow activate PKD1/PKD2 on ECs and this mechanism contributes to the flow-mediated vasodilation. In summary, we show that Wnts are autocrine/paracrine vasodilator proteins. Intravascular flow stimulates ECs to secrete Wnts, which then act via PKD1/PKD2 and Frizzled receptors on ECs to induce vasodilation.

articles_hidden.title: Vegetation decay enhances terrestrial nitrous acid emissions through nitrate reduction
articles_hidden.authors: Jingwei Zhang, Dianming Wu, Yifei Liu, Yuyao Qin, Shiyang Yu, Jitao Lv, Linqian Li, Wei Li, Chaofan Lian, Haiyan Ran, Lingling Deng, Yi Chen, Ruhai Wang, Zehua Fu, Min Liu, Weili Lin, Chaoyang Xue, Maofa Ge, Yongchun Liu, Weigang Wang, Junling An, Dawei Lu, Markku Kulmala, Qiang Zhang, Gui-Bin Jiang
articles_hidden.abstract: Photolysis of nitrous acid (HONO) drives ozone and secondary aerosol formation, yet its sources remain poorly constrained. We identify HONO emissions from decaying aboveground plant residues as a previously overlooked plant-derived component of terrestrial HONO emissions. Field observations and dual-isotope ( 15 N– 18 O) tracing reveal that HONO arises mainly from nitrate reduction within decomposing plants. We integrated global datasets on vegetation nitrate, litter decomposition, soil, and climate to estimate HONO emissions from vegetation decay at 1.1 ± 0.1 Tg N y −1 . This substantially narrows the long-standing uncertainty in HONO budget. This plant-mediated pathway extends the soil-atmosphere paradigm to soil-plant-atmosphere framework. Moreover, we identify emission hotspots and drivers, assess their climate-driven shifts, and propose region-specific mitigation strategies. These findings uncover a missing link between terrestrial nitrogen cycling and atmospheric reactivity, highlighting biogeochemical controls on air quality.

articles_hidden.title: Gaussian mixture model–based focused refinement for enhanced flexible structure determination in CryoEM and CryoET
articles_hidden.authors: Muyuan Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Dynamic conformational changes of proteins are crucial for their cellular functions. Here we present a unified refinement pipeline for flexible protein structures in both CryoEM and in situ CryoET. Using a Gaussian mixture model–based focused alignment procedure, we improve resolution of small domains in highly dynamic proteins and reveal intricate conformational changes. The method corrects the per-subunit motion of TRPV1 and captures the rotary dynamics of ATP synthase within mitochondria.

articles_hidden.title: A decavalent Group B streptococcal biosynthetic conjugate vaccine provides functional immunity to all known serotypes
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel L. Edwards, Kathleen N. McAllister, Isra Darwech, Jenna C. McGuffey, Cory J. Knoot, Nathan Pomper, Lloyd S. Robinson, Anna J. Hooppaw, Stephen Thomas, Kostis Apostolakis, Ashley Shepherd, Stephen Taylor, Paeton L. Wantuch, David A. Rosen, Nichollas E. Scott, Christian M. Harding
articles_hidden.abstract: Globally, 394,000 cases of Group B Streptococcus (GBS) infection occur each year, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Vaccination has emerged as an important strategy to limit GBS infections and disease; however, existing vaccine candidates currently in clinical development do not cover all capsular polysaccharide serotypes. Here, we describe the use of a next generation bioconjugation platform to generate a decavalent GBS vaccine (GBS10V) and characterize its immunological evaluation in animals. Using an evolved PglS bioconjugation platform, capsular polysaccharides from all 10 GBS capsular polysaccharide serotypes were individually expressed and bioconjugated to an optimized Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin A (EPA6) carrier protein engineered with six sequons. Multiple biochemical analyses confirmed the identity of each polysaccharide serotype bioconjugated to EPA6. Moreover, intact mass spectrometry (MS) and MS/MS spectra confirmed the presence of sialic acid in each repeat unit of GBS polysaccharides attached to the carrier, an attribute critical for eliciting an optimal immune response. The GBS10V vaccine was used to immunize outbred CD-1 mice and New Zealand White rabbits with doses of 1, 2, or 5 μg per GBS serotype. Sera analyses demonstrated the GBS10V vaccine induced high serotype-specific immunoglobulin titers to all 10 serotypes. Most importantly, interim and postimmune sera from rabbits demonstrated potent opsonophagocytic killing, with median titers ranging from 646 to 6,145 for all serotypes by day 42. Together, these findings establish GBS10V as a global GBS conjugate vaccine candidate for all patient populations, and thus, justify its further preclinical development.

articles_hidden.title: Universal scaling in the rheology of dense cellular systems
articles_hidden.authors: Helen S. Ansell, Daniel M. Sussman
articles_hidden.abstract: Biological tissues must dynamically transition between solid-like and fluid-like states during processes like morphogenesis and collective migration, often while resisting physiological shear stresses. It remains unclear whether these transitions in tissue dynamics are governed by the same nonequilibrium critical phenomena that control conventional disordered matter. Here we show that the flow response of model cell monolayers under constant shear stress is described by universal scaling behavior, with different flow regimes controlled by the same underlying physical parameters. This framework captures regimes in which the underlying system has both rigid and fluid-like behavior in the absence of imposed fluctuations and stresses. In the rigid regime, small internal fluctuations maintain a solid-like state up to a finite yield stress before the tissue shear thins; the fluid-like regime instead exhibits robust continuous and discontinuous shear thickening. We demonstrate that at high enough stress, the fluid-like regime undergoes structural arrest. This space-filling shear-jamming transition is accompanied by structural changes, including the formation of system-spanning force chains and the emergence of orientational ordering. These results establish confluent tissues as a distinct class of disordered matter, demonstrating that complex nonlinear rheology and structural arrest can emerge entirely through shape-driven topological constraints to regulate biological mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: ZCWPW1 organizes telomeric architecture to drive meiotic chromosome movements
articles_hidden.authors: Wenxin Xie, Manjunath Gowder, Dominic Bazzano, Adrienne Niederriter Shami, Aastha Pandey, Melissa Frasca, Lakshmi Paniker, Luciana Previato de Almeida, Binod Kumar Bharati, Jing Liang, Pankaj Vilas Jadhav, Elizabeth Finn, Attila Tóth, Morgan DeSantis, Jayakrishnan Nandakumar, Evgeny Nudler, Shyamal Mosalaganti, Roberto J. Pezza, Francesca Cole, Saher Sue Hammoud
articles_hidden.abstract: Proper meiotic homolog pairing requires the coordination of two processes: DNA recombination and chromosome-scale mechanical movements. Here, we identify a dual role in both meiotic processes for the chromatin reader ZCWPW1 in mouse spermatocytes. The current dogma proposes that ZCWPW1 acts downstream of PRDM9, reading the PRDM9-deposited H3K4 and K36me3 modifications at recombination hotspots and promoting DSB repair. Using superresolution imaging, we show that ZCWPW1 is diffuse throughout the nucleus but enriched at the nuclear periphery near TRF1, LINC complex components, and dynein. ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN further confirms its genomic enrichment at subtelomeric regions. Loss of ZCWPW1 disrupts telomere architecture, weakens telomere-LINC-motor coupling, and markedly reduces chromosome movement. These defects are more severe than, and mechanistically independent of, those observed in Prdm9 −/− spermatocytes. Together, our data reveal an unexpected PRDM9-independent role for ZCWPW1 as an intranuclear regulator of both recombination and mechanical movements that coordinate to drive efficient homolog pairing.

articles_hidden.title: Temperature-dependent kinetic isotope effects in methane reactions with OH and Cl reshape atmospheric sink fractionation
articles_hidden.authors: Marie Kathrine Mikkelsen, Jacob Lynge Elholm, Sergey Gromov, Thomas Röckmann, Gunnar Nyman, Kurt V. Mikkelsen, Matthew S. Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: The abundances of stable isotopes in methane (CH 4 ) are used to distinguish fossil and biological emissions and to constrain the global methane budget. While these analyses require correction for isotopic fractionation occurring in methane’s atmospheric reactions, the temperature dependence of the kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) are poorly described and typically ignored. Here we combine density functional theory, Møller–Plesset perturbation theory, coupled-cluster calculations, and tunneling-corrected transition state theory to develop a first-principles description of the temperature-dependent KIEs for CH 4 and its isotopologues reacting with OH and Cl over the range 100 to 500 K which exhibit substantial and previously neglected temperature dependence. Incorporation of these KIEs into the EMAC chemistry–climate model yields systematically different effective atmospheric sink fractionation factors than those obtained using temperature-invariant values. The largest differences occur for chlorine oxidation in the cold upper troposphere and stratosphere, where methane isotope budgets are particularly sensitive to reactive halogens. We find a weak 13 C–D clumping anomaly and a strong D–D clumping anomaly, confirming earlier work and demonstrating that atmospheric oxidation produces substantial enrichment in Δ 12 CH 2 D 2 , and helping to reconcile source signatures with atmospheric observations. These results show that temperature-dependent KIEs are required for robust interpretation of methane isotopes in both contemporary and past atmospheres.

articles_hidden.title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
articles_hidden.authors: Veronica Tollenaar, Etienne Legrain
articles_hidden.abstract: Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.

articles_hidden.title: A sweeping twist defect as a topological flagellum that enhances colloid translation
articles_hidden.authors: Qi Xing Zhang, Claire Doré, Mojtaba Rajabi, Edward Brian Steager, Kathleen J. Stebe
articles_hidden.abstract: Nematic liquid crystals can dramatically reconfigure under dynamic forcing, providing exciting opportunities in active matter. Here, we study a disk colloid with hybrid planar and homeotropic anchoring rotated by an external magnetic field which generates a dynamic companion topological defect. The disk moves faster when the defect sweeps across the disk’s face. We identify the defect as a nonsingular twist wall, characterize the twist energy landscape, and identify that the sweeping motion is driven by a topological instability. As the defect sweeps, it reverses the handedness of twist and lowers the free energy in the fluid in the gap above the disk. Landau–de Gennes modeling shows that the sweeping wall behaves as a propagating director texture: the director field is nearly stationary in the wall frame, while nematogens rotate locally as the wall passes. The nematogens’ rotation generates a viscous stress on the surface of the disk that hastens its propulsion. Thus, the defect acts as a flagellum that powers colloid swimming, providing an example of a dissipative topological structure whose dynamics can be harnessed to perform useful work.

articles_hidden.title: Modulating chain conformations and hydrogen-bond dynamics at silica–rubber interfaces for enhanced energy dissipation in composites
articles_hidden.authors: Longjin Huang, Xiaomin Song, Yang Yang, Zhaoqun Shao, Changlin Li, Fengmei Yu, Ai Lu, Shichun Li, Xueyan Zhao, Ping Zhang, Sheng Cui, Chunhua Zhu, Yu Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: The polymer–nanoparticle interphase is essential for fabricating high-performance nanocomposites, as it dictates mechanical properties through interfacial stress transfer and energy dissipation. However, engineering the buried interphases remains challenging due to the complex hierarchical structure and methodological limitations, particularly in silica–rubber systems where confined polymer chain conformation and hydrogen-bond dynamics are poorly resolved. Herein, a selective polymer-removal technique was developed to strip free and loosely bound polymer under extreme conditions, enabling TEM visualization of polymer chain-like interfacial features consistent with train-, loop-, and tail-like adsorption motifs in silica/silicone rubber nanocomposites. Correlative analysis combining STEM-EELS, high-resolution NMR, in situ variable-temperature IR, and 2D low-field NMR spectroscopy resolves hydrogen bonding between silica surface hydroxyls and silicone backbone oxygen atoms (Si-O-H···O-Si), which exhibit temperature-dependent behavior. Quantitative analysis reveals the strategic modulation of interphase layer thickness: As the apparent hydroxyl density of silica varied from 2.1 to 12.9 OH nm −2 , the interphase thickness increased from 4.1 ± 0.8 nm to 13.2 ± 1.4 nm (9.5 mol% polymer phenyl); increasing the polymer phenyl content to 29.7 mol% further expands the layer to 23.4 ± 1.0 nm. Molecular dynamics simulations also suggest that higher silica surface hydroxyl density enhances multipoint adsorption of polymer chain, which promotes the formation of loop and train conformations. These confined chain arrangements are consistent with the reduced Arrhenius activation energy from 101 to 50 kJ mol −1 measured by dynamic rheology, which facilitates interfacial chain mobility and hydrogen-bond exchange during deformation. These findings provide molecular-level insights for the rational design of polymer nanocomposites.

articles_hidden.title: Tumor cell–intrinsic E47 functions as a critical suppressor in antitumor immunity via the FBXL2–PD-L1 axis
articles_hidden.authors: Rongtian Guo, Kun Wang, Jing Xu, Xin Lian, Ruixiao Bai, Xiaoli Chen, Haorui Zheng, Jiexin Gao, Yong Yi, Zhi-Xiong Jim Xiao, Mengmeng Niu
articles_hidden.abstract: The transcription factor E47, encoded by the TCF3 gene, is essential for B and T cell lineage commitment and development. However, whether tumor cell–intrinsic E47 contributes to tumor immunosurveillance remains unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that E47 functions as a critical suppressor of antitumor immunity. Clinical analyses reveal that increased intratumoral TCF3 expression is associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Silencing of E47 in tumor cells markedly inhibits tumor growth, increases infiltration of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, and decreases PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, E47 transcriptionally represses FBXL2 , which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes PD-L1 polyubiquitination at K270 and proteasomal degradation. Restoration of FBXL2 effectively reverses E47-induced PD-L1 upregulation and tumor growth. Strikingly, Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug nebivolol, an activator of FBXL2, significantly enhances antitumor immunity and improves the efficacy of CTLA-4 blockade therapy in syngeneic tumor mouse models. Together, this study uncovers the E47–FBXL2 axis as a critical pathway governing PD-L1 stability and antitumor immunity, highlighting its therapeutic potential for improving the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Phosphorylation-dependent ATPase activity regulates subunit shuffling dynamics in cyanobacterial circadian clock proteins
articles_hidden.authors: Tian Yang, Zhuangcheng Zhen, Ying Luan, Yuhai Tu, Qi Ouyang, Yuansheng Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Protein complexes are essential for cellular functions, with their dynamics increasingly recognized as key regulatory elements. In the cyanobacterial circadian clock, the KaiC hexamer is highly dynamic, undergoing phosphorylation-dependent monomer shuffling that synchronizes individual oscillators. However, the molecular mechanism of monomer shuffling is not fully understood. Here we combine a chromatography-based method with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to quantify subunit exchange in the hexamerization domain of KaiC (KaiC-CI) and in full-length KaiC. We show that ATPase activity is essential for monomer shuffling. Through quantitative modeling of experimental data, we found that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis at two independent monomer–monomer interfaces disassembles a KaiC-CI hexamer into two oligomers. Two complementary oligomers from two different hexamers can rapidly reform a mixed hexamer. Mechanistically, ATP hydrolysis induces unstable, shuffling-competent states in hexamers, while nucleotide exchange stabilizes them, suppressing shuffling. The balance between these two processes quantitatively explains the relationship between shuffling rate and ATPase activity across KaiC mutants observed in our experiments. Applying this model to full-length KaiC revealed that phosphorylation of the KaiC-CII domain modulates shuffling primarily by affecting the nucleotide exchange rate in the CI domain. This establishes a feedback loop where CII phosphorylation alters CI ATPase activity, which in turn controls subunit exchange to synchronize CII phosphorylation across the KaiC hexamer population. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework linking ATPase-driven subunit exchange to the robustness of circadian clocks, with implications for activation-coupled dynamics in other molecular machines.

articles_hidden.title: NSP1–SAMD9L interactions govern murine rotavirus host range restriction in vivo
articles_hidden.authors: Gaopeng Hou, Mei Ren, Wenhao O. Ouyang, Jiang Tan, Constin Liu, Yinxing Zhu, Qiru Zeng, Yidan Sun, Nicholas C. Wu, Siyuan Ding
articles_hidden.abstract: Rotavirus replication, pathogenesis, and transmission are host-range restricted, yet the viral and host determinants remain poorly defined. Rotavirus nonstructural protein 1 (NSP1) is a multifunctional innate immune antagonist dispensable for replication in permissive cells. Here, using reverse genetics, neonatal mice, intestinal organoids, and comparative proteomics, we identify mouse SAMD9L as a critical host restriction factor selectively antagonized by murine rotavirus-encoded NSP1. An NSP1-deletion murine-like rotavirus produced progeny efficiently in cell lines but was highly attenuated in neonatal mice with no productive intestinal replication, fecal shedding, and diarrhea. Recombinant monoreassortant viruses carrying NSP1 genes from rhesus, bovine, or human rotavirus strains did not support murine intestinal infection, even in Stat1 −/− pups, indicating an additional restriction mechanism beyond STAT1-dependent antiviral signaling. Comparative proteomics identified mouse SAMD9L as a specific interactor of murine NSP1, and NSP1 promoted SAMD9L degradation through a neddylation- and proteasome-dependent pathway. AlphaFold3 guided mutagenesis identified NSP1 residues S364/E366 and SAMD9L residues R455/L462 as functionally important for the NSP1–SAMD9L interaction. Mutations on either side disrupted NSP1–SAMD9L association and prevented SAMD9L degradation. Replication of murine rotaviruses carrying S364A or E366A mutations was undetectable in wild-type mice and was restored in Samd9l −/− mice. Combined deletion of Samd9l and Stat1 permitted replication of otherwise attenuated viruses carrying mismatched NSP1s and enabled fecal IgA seroconversion after a single oral inoculation of Rotarix. These findings identify SAMD9L as a physiologically relevant intestinal restriction factor in mice and show that murine NSP1 antagonism of mouse SAMD9L contributes to murine rotavirus host range restriction in vivo.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised Bayesian neural networks enable inference of complex epidemiological and macroevolutionary processes
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriele Marino, Ugnė Stolz, Cecilia Valenzuela Agüí, Tanja Stadler, Daniele Silvestro
articles_hidden.abstract: Birth–death models quantify macroevolutionary and epidemiological processes, including speciation, extinction, and transmission, based on phylogenetic trees. Extensions of these models incorporate external covariates as predictors of these parameters, for instance linking traits or environmental variables with changes in these rates. However, the dependencies between predictors and model parameters are typically restricted to linear, additive effects and may thus fail to capture complex, nonlinear relationships underlying evolutionary dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that leverages unsupervised Bayesian neural networks to flexibly model functional relationships between these parameters and a broad set of predictors, including categorical traits, quantitative variables, and time series data. Based on these covariates, the network weights and thus the resulting birth–death dynamics are estimated jointly with the phylogenetic tree, obtained directly from sequence alignment data. Extensive simulations show that this approach accurately recovers predictor–parameter relationships, mitigates overfitting, and remains robust across both macroevolutionary and epidemiological contexts. Using explainable AI, we further show that our framework reliably identifies the most influential predictors and yields interpretable descriptions of their impact on the inferred rates. Finally, we apply our method in two empirical analyses: linking SARS-CoV-2 migration dynamics with travel data during its early spread in Europe, and inferring trait- and time-dependent speciation and extinction rates in the diversification of platyrrhines. Our framework substantially expands the capabilities of birth–death models, providing a powerful and flexible approach to infer complex epidemiological and macroevolutionary processes.

articles_hidden.title: Pinning of Van Hove singularities and correlated insulators in M-valley twisted transition metal dichalcogenides
articles_hidden.authors: Christophe De Beule, Liangtao Peng, Eugene J. Mele, Shaffique Adam
articles_hidden.abstract: We investigate the role of long-range Coulomb interactions in M-valley moirés using the self-consistent Hartree–Fock approximation. This platform was recently proposed [D. Călugăru et al., Nature 643 , 376–381 (2025) and C. Lei et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135 , 196402 (2025)] as a new class of experimentally realizable moiré materials using twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) homobilayers with the 1T structure. While these seminal studies considered the noninteracting theory without an electric displacement field, this work shows that both electron–electron interactions at finite doping and an interlayer bias strongly modify the moiré bands. For small twists ( ≲ 5°) the density of states versus filling and interlayer bias displays qualitatively different behavior for twisting near aligned (0°) and antialigned (60°) stacking with tunable Van Hove singularities (VHSs). Moreover, interactions pin the VHS to the Fermi energy over a finite range of doping both at zero and finite bias depending on the stacking type, an effect known to enhance both superconductivity and strongly correlated states. At half-filling, we obtain the phase diagram as a function of interaction strength, interlayer bias, and twist angle. We find a competition driven by band mixing between an isotropic ferromagnet and an antiferromagnet that are nearly degenerate over a wide range of experimentally accessible parameters. Our work demonstrates that correlated states in M-valley twisted TMD homobilayers can be strongly tuned in situ both by applying an electric displacement field and by electron doping.

articles_hidden.abstract: Neuropathic pain involves persistent metabolic and transcriptional remodeling in spinal microglia, but the mechanisms linking these processes remain unclear. Microglia-specific Prmt5 deletion or pharmacological inhibition reduced glycolytic remodeling and pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, PRMT5 associated with alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1), promoted AARS1-associated symmetric dimethylation and nuclear accumulation, and supported AARS1-dependent H3K18la and H4K12la. Disrupting AARS1 nuclear localization impaired histone lactylation and glycolytic responses. The pathway was validated in primary microglia, spinal microglia, and female mice. articles_hidden.title: Contrasting spatial homogeneity in atmospheric ice-nucleating particles from local to synoptic scales
articles_hidden.authors: Ruichen Zhou, Drew Juergensen, Kelton Ayars, Carson Hume, Kevin Barry, Oren Dutton, Gavin McMeeking, Ezra Levin, Anna Hodshire, Leah Gibson, Ethan Emerson, Paul J. DeMott, Jessie M. Creamean, Sonia Kreidenweis, Russell Perkins
articles_hidden.abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) play a critical role in regulating glaciation and precipitation formation in mixed-phase cloud (containing liquid and ice), yet their spatial variability across different scales remains poorly constrained. At these scales, INP concentrations were generally spatially homogeneous during each campaign, indicating that single-site measurements can often represent surrounding areas. Extending the analysis to the synoptic scale across multiple campaigns, warm-temperature INPs showed greater site-to-site differences, suggesting stronger influences from local or regional sources. In contrast, INPs active at colder temperatures showed much stronger spatial similarity between two inland continental sites separated by 800 km, revealing a broader regional coherence in this INP population. This was also observed at the coastal site, but only under continental air mass influence; the similarity weakened under marine air masses. These results suggest that cold-temperature INPs may reflect a broader INP background over continents such as that contributed by windblown dust. Our findings provide direct observational constraints on the representativeness of single-site INP measurements, which can help inform the strategy for representing variations in INP populations in atmospheric models.

articles_hidden.title: Rural outdoor air pollution exceeds urban levels in the Delhi megacity region
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Joseph Campmier, Sofiya Rao, Amarendra Singh, Saumya Singh, María Teresa Hernández, Nidhi Malik, Swagata Dey, Ajay Pillarisetti, Kalpana Balakrishnan, Sagnik Dey, Joshua S. Apte
articles_hidden.abstract: India routinely experiences some of the highest concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) air pollution in the world. Although India’s population predominantly lives in rural areas and smaller cities, policy efforts to date have emphasized air pollution in India’s large cities. In contrast, there is limited understanding of air pollutant dynamics in India’s rural and less urbanized areas. Here, we established a well-calibrated lower-cost PM 2.5 sensor network spanning a wide range of urbanicity (population densities: 300 to 30,000 people/km 2 ) outside and inside of Delhi. The network of 49 sites incorporated a 160 km measurement transect to capture ambient PM 2.5 trends of the Delhi megacity, as well as stratified measurements in villages, small cities, and Delhi itself. We report on data from 5 mo of operation (July–November 2024) spanning the cleanest and most polluted times of the year. PM 2.5 concentrations at rural sites consistently exceeded those at urban sites by about 20% during every month of our study. Analysis of diurnal PM 2.5 cycles showed sharp morning (approximately 06:00–10:00 LT) and evening (approximately 16:00–20:00 LT) concentration peaks at rural sites that were absent at urban sites. We attribute these events to widespread use of solid fuels for cooking, heating, and small-scale industry in suburban and rural settings. These striking enhancements in rural air pollution are missed by satellite remote sensing data, and our findings run contrary to the general societal perception that Indian cities are pollution hotspots relative to rural areas.

articles_hidden.title: Structural and biochemical impact of clinically relevant constitutively active parathyroid hormone receptor 1 mutations
articles_hidden.authors: Isabella C. Russell, Elita Yuliantie, Zamara Mariam, Hariprasad Venogupal, George Christopoulos, Xin Zhang, Brian P. Cary, Christopher Phillips, Arjan Snijder, Taianá Maia de Oliveira, Giuseppe Deganutti, Matthew J. Belousoff, Patrick M. Sexton, Denise Wootten
articles_hidden.abstract: Parathyroid hormone receptor 1 (PTH1R) constitutively active mutants, including H223 2.50 R and T410 6.42 P, are responsible for Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, a form of short-limbed dwarfism. Here, we expand pharmacological understanding and present cryoelectron microscopy structures of the constitutively active PTH1R mutants, H223 2.50 K, H223 2.50 R, and T410 6.42 P, in complex with Gs protein and PTH(1–34), and H223 2.50 R and T410 6.42 P in the ligand free Gs complexed form. These reveal modifications in polar networks that allow for constitutive G protein coupling and subsequent signaling. In the absence of a peptide bound to the extracellular side of the PTH1R, TM6 adopts a distinct conformation relative to the PTH(1–34) bound wild-type PTH1R coupled with Gs. Combined with molecular dynamics analysis of inactive and Gs bound receptors, this work reveals distinct mechanisms that lead to differing receptor activation states and consequently promote distinct constitutive activity and agonist-mediated pharmacological profiles.

articles_hidden.title: Precursor-engineered lithiation kinetics enable low-temperature synthesis of Li–Ni–O positive electrode materials
articles_hidden.authors: Chenguang Shi, Junyi Yao, Elliot Brim, Sooyeon Hwang, Xiaowen Zhan, Yaobin Xu, Hongyu Wang, Changlian Wen, Dali Yang, Lu Ma, Sizhan Liu, Hui Zhong, Jianming Bai, Gihan Kwon, Molleigh Preefer, Dennis Nordlund, Jordi Cabana, Ryan M. Richards, Jie Xiao, Feng Lin
articles_hidden.abstract: High-nickel cathodes provide high capacity in lithium-ion batteries; however, their slow lithiation reactions require a prolonged high-temperature hold during synthesis which is directly responsible for high manufacturing cost. Here, we report that the precursor morphology and crystallinity can be engineered to regulate the nucleation and growth of the layered phase at temperatures as low as 575 °C. We use nanosheets of NiO and Ni(OH) 2 with high specific surface areas to maximize the contact area between Li and Ni precursors and to shorten Li + diffusion lengths. Highly crystalline NiO seeds early and uniform layered phase nucleation at low temperatures. Preheating Ni(OH) 2 to NiO at 300 °C maintains the large surface area and yields a higher layered fraction with limited lamellae coarsening. Preheating at 500 °C produces more crystalline NiO seeds that promote the synchronous Ni oxidation and cation ordering upon layered phase formation to deliver higher discharge capacity and better rate capability than conventionally synthesized LiNiO 2 . In contrast, along the hydroxide-based route, in situ generated Li 2 CO 3 disrupts wetting and hampers lithiation, ultimately trapping lithium within a disordered rocksalt intermediate. This work demonstrates that precursor morphology, crystallinity, and processing temperature control lithiation kinetics, providing broad guidance for energy-efficient synthesizing advanced oxide battery cathodes.

articles_hidden.title: Immunometabolic basis of glutamine supplementation as a potential host-directed therapy for tuberculosis
articles_hidden.authors: Qingkui Jiang, Ryan J. Dikdan, Yunping Qiu, Wei Wang, Joseph J. Bulatowicz, Victor C. Agbara, Irwin J. Kurland, Luke Fritzky, Youssef Sabha, Dongfang Liu, Sanjay Tyagi, Selvakumar Subbian, Karl Drlica, Lanbo Shi
articles_hidden.abstract: Undernutrition is the leading risk factor for tuberculosis susceptibility, severity, and poor treatment outcome. Nutritional immunology and immunometabolism frame how nutrient availability and metabolism shape host defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) infection. By integrating targeted metabolomics and transcriptional profiling in a murine tuberculosis model, we defined immunometabolic programs underlying the transition from acute to chronic infection. Immune control of Mtb during acute infection was accompanied by robust activation of immune and metabolic programs, including mTORC1-associated signaling, glutaminolysis, glycolysis, arginine metabolism, and serine one-carbon metabolism, thereby highlighting the importance of amino acid metabolism and mitochondrial function in antimicrobial immunity. In contrast, chronic infection was characterized by reduced immune activation and mTORC1-associated signaling, increased branched-chain amino acid catabolism, and altered amino acid profiles, with leucine and glutamine among the discriminating metabolites. These findings suggest that reduced glutamine availability during chronic infection may increase reliance on leucine oxidative catabolism to sustain mitochondrial metabolism during nutrient stress, potentially limiting leucine availability for mTORC1-associated anabolic metabolism and immune activation. Oral glutamine supplementation restored amino acid homeostasis, including lung leucine abundance, enhanced mTORC1-associated signaling and central metabolic programs, moderately reduced bacterial burden and lung pathology, and mitigated infection-associated wasting. Reanalysis of published human metabolomics datasets further demonstrated reduced circulating glutamine levels during progression to active tuberculosis, supporting conservation of glutamine metabolic dysregulation across host species. Collectively, our findings identify a potential glutamine–leucine metabolic axis linking nutrient availability with immunometabolic competence and provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating glutamine supplementation as a host-directed strategy for tuberculosis.

articles_hidden.title: Single-cell genomics reveals genome streamlining and functional traits in dominant uncultured marine protists
articles_hidden.authors: David López-Escardó, Aleix Obiol, Guillem Marimon, Xabier López-Alforja, Dolors Vaqué, Irene Forn, Ramiro Logares, Sheree Yau, Òscar Fornas, Manuel Martínez-García, Ramon Massana
articles_hidden.abstract: Marine protists are key players in marine ecosystems, yet a large fraction, particularly among the smallest taxa, belongs to uncultured lineages lacking genomic data, limiting our understanding of their ecology and evolution. Beyond determining their gene repertoires, genomic information is essential to reveal how genomes are organized. Features such as genome size, GC content, and structural gene architecture represent physical constraints that shape evolutionary fitness and adaptability in marine environments. Here, we present a genomic catalog of 147 marine picoplanktonic protist species, greatly expanding the genomic representation of uncultured and ecologically relevant lineages through a single-cell approach. This dataset enables refined phylogenomic placement of previously uncharacterized marine eukaryotes, including abundant marine protistan players as well as a few species belonging to novel or poorly known groups that are crucial for resolving deep questions in eukaryotic evolution. We uncover pronounced genome streamlining in ecologically successful lineages, coupled with extensive, mostly lineage-specific functional adaptations. At a broader scale, we identify functional traits enriched independently across several marine eukaryotic lineages, including genes involved in complex carbohydrate degradation in heterotrophic organisms and the presence of polyketide synthases. Together, these results provide a framework for investigating the genomic drivers and molecular mechanisms behind the ecological success of marine eukaryotic microbes.

articles_hidden.title: A two-dimensional molecular gearbox operated in a crystalline solid
articles_hidden.authors: Hikaru Yamamoto, Rempei Ando, Ayana Sato-Tomita, Masahiro Kuramochi, Motohiro Mizuno, Hiroshi Sekiguchi, Mikhail Tsitsvero, Andrey Lyalin, Tetsuya Taketsugu, Hajime Ito, Mingoo Jin
articles_hidden.abstract: Since the earliest artificial gears, parallel gearbox systems based on intermeshing two-dimensional (2D) networks of multiple gear units have served a fundamental role in macroscale mechanical devices through the correlated mechanical motion of multiple gears. However, the realization of molecular-level 2D gearbox machinery with correlated motion among multiple units remains highly challenging. Here, we report a molecular-level 2D gearbox in a crystal, formed through the supramolecular assembly of an Au(I)-complex rotor with tripodal triptycene and triadamantyl phosphine (Ad 3 P) rotators, connected via an ethynyl–Au(I) unit. Upon heating, the rotators within a 2D hexagonal gear network exhibit 120° site-exchange rotational motion in a correlated manner, as revealed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD), 2 H solid-state (SS) NMR spectroscopy, and time-resolved variable-temperature XRD measurements. In addition, density functional theory calculations provide insight into the energetic preference for correlated motion within the gear-network. This 2D intermolecular gearbox in the crystalline state represents a supramolecular platform in which the intermolecular gearing motion has a large impact on the bulk crystal, which could provide a bridge between molecular-level mechanical properties and macroscale SS physical functions.

articles_hidden.title: Gammaherpesvirus infection drives genotype-dependent virus-specific T cell responses in the CNS prior to autoimmune neuroinflammation
articles_hidden.authors: Katherine J. Sessions, Emily A. Nelson, Rae-Ling Lee, Courtney M. Waytashek, Senjuti Sengupta, Theresa L. Montgomery, Edward J. Usherwood, Anthony J. Filiano, Dimitry N. Krementsov
articles_hidden.abstract: Infection with the gammaherpesvirus Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is the strongest environmental risk factor for multiple sclerosis (MS). This risk is driven by poor immune control of viral replication, which is genetically determined. Clonally expanded CD8 T cells are abundant in MS lesions, and some recognize EBV antigens. We previously demonstrated that host genetic variation regulates immune control of the homologous B cell–tropic murine gammaherpesvirus, MHV-68. Here, we investigated how gammaherpesvirus infection and host genotype shape central nervous system (CNS) T cell responses, before and after induction of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Chronic infection alone was sufficient to promote a marked accumulation of CX3CR1+KLRG1+ effector CD8 T cells and CX3CR1+KLRG1+ cytotoxic-like T helper cells in the CNS of MHV-68-susceptible C57BL/6 mice. T cells localized to brain border regions and throughout the CNS parenchyma. MHC tetramer analysis demonstrated that CNS-infiltrating T cells were specific for viral antigens, and viral DNA was detectable in CNS-infiltrating leukocytes during early and chronic infection. EAE further amplified cytotoxic T cell accumulation in the CNS of MHV-68-infected C57BL/6 mice. However, CNS T cell infiltration was highly attenuated in genetically divergent wild-derived PWD/PhJ mice, which control MHV-68 more effectively, but not in MHV-68-susceptible 129S1/SvImJ mice. Surprisingly, chronic MHV-68 infection modestly delayed EAE onset in C57BL/6 mice, an effect reversed by B cell depletion. Together with emerging human studies, our results suggest that host genetic variation contributes to poor control of EBV in MS, promoting virus-specific cytotoxic T cell accumulation in the CNS and immune reprogramming both before and during autoimmune neuroinflammation.

articles_hidden.title: Soil contamination and acidification jointly increased cereal cadmium and dietary exposure over four decades
articles_hidden.authors: Qi-Xin Lü, Shuyou Zhang, Lili Niu, Pengjie Hu, Zhi-Xian Tang, Ya-Di Yang, Wangbo Zhang, Yongming Luo, Fang-Jie Zhao, Yijun Yao, Peng Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Cadmium contamination of staple cereals is an important food-safety concern, yet how long-term changes in soil chemistry alter cadmium transfer into food remains poorly resolved. Here we reconstructed changes in cropland topsoil cadmium and pH across China from 1980 to 2020 and quantified their consequences for cereal grain cadmium, dietary exposure, and mitigation potential. National mean topsoil cadmium increased from 0.123 to 0.236 mg kg −1 , while mean cropland pH declined from 6.50 to 6.30 nationally and by about 0.5 units in several southern rice-growing provinces. These coupled changes increased mean grain cadmium from 0.043 to 0.100 mg kg −1 in rice and from 0.017 to 0.032 mg kg −1 in wheat. By 2020, provinces with estimated mean hazard quotients exceeded 1.0 had a combined population of about 138 million. Counterfactual analysis showed that soil cadmium accumulation remained the dominant driver of rising grain cadmium, while acidification substantially amplified soil-to-grain transfer, especially in rice systems. Scenario analysis to 2050 indicated that restoring cropland pH to 6.5 could offset about 44% of the projected increase in rice cadmium even without immediate source control, whereas combining pH restoration with source control reduced mean rice cadmium by about 59% and brought exceedance close to zero. These findings identify soil acidification as an important amplifier of cadmium transfer into staple cereals and highlight targeted cropland pH restoration as a practical near-term strategy for reducing food-chain exposure while longer-term source-control measures take effect.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond blood ammonia: Intestinal ammonia emerges as an early microbial driver of mild cognitive impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Hao Chen, Zhen Wang, Yajun Tang, Yahui Liu, Lihui Kou, Jing Huang, Ke Guo, Zheng Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an early and potentially reversible stage of neurodegenerative disease, yet its initiating pathogenic signal remains unclear. Here, we identify gut microbiota-derived, urease-dependent intestinal ammonia as an early functional contributor to cognitive impairment. Analyses of human MCI-related cohorts revealed increased fecal urease activity and ammonia-related microbial features associated with cognitive performance. Importantly, intestinal ammonia accumulation precedes detectable elevations in blood ammonia, indicating that local intestinal dysregulation occurs before systemic hyperammonemia. Mechanistically, ammonia suppresses colonic SMAD7 and activates JAK2 signaling in the brain, thereby promoting cognitive dysfunction independently of systemic ammonia toxicity. This signaling pattern was further supported in 5xFAD mice. Therapeutically, supplementation with the ammonia-assimilating bacterium Limosilactobacillus mucosae or treatment with the clinically used ammonia-lowering agent L-ornithine-L-aspartate reduces intestinal ammonia levels and ameliorates early cognitive deficits. Together, these findings define an ammonia-SMAD7-JAK2 axis linking gut metabolism to brain function and highlight intestinal ammonia as a promising therapeutic target for early cognitive impairment.

articles_hidden.title: An alternative patterning mechanism for vertebrate tooth complexity
articles_hidden.authors: Daria Razmadze, Juuso Ikola, Ida-Maria Aalto, Nicolas Di-Poï
articles_hidden.abstract: How development reliably generates complex patterns remains a central question in biology. Teeth provide an ideal system for addressing this problem, linking cusp-patterning mechanisms to diversification and the fossil record, yet the developmental basis of multicuspid crown patterning beyond mammals remains unresolved. In mammals, cusp initiation and spacing are controlled by transient epithelial signaling centers called enamel knots (EKs). Here, we combine comparative developmental analyses, 3D morphometrics, mutant perturbation, and Bayesian inverse modeling (BITES; Bayesian Inference for Tooth Emergence Simulation) to examine tooth morphogenesis across six squamate species representing convergent multicuspid dentitions. We find that cusp patterning in these taxa does not rely on a discrete EK-based patterning system. Instead, cusps arise from a broad, persistent cusp signaling field (CSF) that deploys canonical tooth-patterning pathways but lacks the spatial restriction, apoptosis, and discrete secondary EKs (SEKs) characteristic of the mammalian system. Changes in epithelial growth and signaling are associated with disproportionate expansion of this field during tooth development and with the formation of additional cusps. Quantitative variation in field extent and dynamics can generate crown morphologies within and across species, providing a developmental basis for positional heterodonty and repeated gains and losses of multicuspidity in squamates. Our results identify an alternative epithelial patterning architecture for vertebrate cusp formation, in which conserved tooth-patterning signals are deployed through a broad field-based architecture rather than compact signaling centers. Together, these findings revise how tooth developmental complexity is encoded and show how similar complex crown forms can evolve through distinct flexible epithelial patterning mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Human sperm mitochondrial DNA retention is associated with reduced fecundability
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey M. Mann, Karolina Nowak, Savni Sawant, Ricardo P. Bertolla, J. Richard Pilsner
articles_hidden.abstract: Maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is thought to depend in part on elimination of paternal mtDNA during spermatogenesis, yet elevated sperm mtDNA copy number (mtDNAcn) is associated with reduced semen quality and longer time-to-pregnancy (TTP). Whether this reflects mtDNA retained within mature sperm or somatic-cell contamination remains unresolved. Here, we used digital PCR and an adapted mtDNA FISH in mature sperm among normospermic men in a prospective preconception pregnancy cohort. We directly visualized mtDNA in the sperm midpiece, and imaging-based mtDNA signal corresponded with bulk sperm mtDNAcn, supporting a sperm-intrinsic origin. Sperm mtDNA retention increased across mtDNAcn groups associated with lower fecundability, reflecting both higher proportion of mtDNA-positive sperm and greater midpiece signal. Substantial cell-to-cell heterogeneity suggests elevated bulk mtDNAcn reflects a distinct subpopulation of mtDNA-retaining sperm. These findings provide direct cellular evidence of mtDNA retention in a subset of mature human sperm and identify mtDNA retention as a sperm phenotype associated with lower fecundability despite normal semen parameters. More broadly, they refine current models of mitochondrial genome elimination during human spermatogenesis and provide cellular context for sperm mtDNAcn as a marker of fecundability.

articles_hidden.title: Pyrethroid insecticide exposure enhances the ability of Helicoverpa armigera to counter host plant defenses through symbiotic bacteria
articles_hidden.authors: Meng Gu, Qiong Yang, Amosi Leonard Mbuji, Jing Yu, Rujing Kang, Lulu Zhang, Yuhao Cai, Laixin Luo, Ary A. Hoffmann, Lei Zhang, Pei Liang
articles_hidden.abstract: Like plant toxins, synthetic insecticides can exert strong selective pressures on pest populations. While responses to both plant toxins and synthetic insecticides can depend on adaptive changes in the nuclear genotype of the pest species, increasing evidence suggests that symbiotic microbes, particularly gut microbes, can also influence these responses. In the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera , concentrations of the symbiont Corynebacterium glyciniphilum increased in moth strains that were treated with the pyrethroid pesticide lambda-cyhalothrin (LCH), and they were also high in LCH-resistant strains and in populations exposed to 2-Tridecanone (2-TD), a secondary defense compound that is present in the Solanaceae. This increase enhanced the ability of H. armigera to overcome not only the pesticide but also a key defense mechanism in the solanaceous plants. In field populations of H. armigera , the abundance of C. glyciniphilum was lowest in populations feeding on nonsolanaceous plants that were sensitive to LCH. Based on gene knockouts, the underlying reason for the enhanced defensive capability provided by C. glyciniphilum was attributed to two detoxification enzyme genes (a P450 cytochrome and an esterase ) which can metabolize both LCH and 2-TD into nontoxic degradation products. These findings suggest that a common mechanism mediated by a symbiont contributes to the insect’s capacity to develop resistance to both a pesticide and a host plant toxin.

articles_hidden.title: Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama’s anchoveta fishery and its exports
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew J. Sellers, Carolina Chong-Montenegro, Amber L. Carter, Anabell J. Cornejo, Natasha A. Hinojosa, Javier Pardo Díaz, Anastasia Quintana, Ramiro Solís, Ana K. Spalding, Aaron O’Dea
articles_hidden.abstract: In 2025 the seasonal upwelling of the Gulf of Panama failed. Net primary production fell by 64% across the Gulf and industrial anchoveta landings dropped to 11% of the average, the lowest since the fishery became fully exploited in 1966. Anchoveta caught per purse-seine set fell to under a third of the normal rate while total catch per set stayed within its normal range. Landed fish carried about half their usual lipid content, and fish oil exports fell by 88% in both volume and value. The effects of one failed season reached international trade within months. Seasonal upwellings like this are common across the tropics yet far less studied than the large eastern boundary systems. The very strong El Niño now under way makes the 2027 season more uncertain.

articles_hidden.title: Targeted metabolic reprogramming of CD8 T cells restores immune regulation in lupus
articles_hidden.authors: Seiya Oba, Morgane H. Humbel, Hyshem H. Lancia, Wei Li, Wenliang Pan, Vasileios C. Kyttaris, Mohammad Rashidian, Reza Abdi, Maria G. Tsokos, George C. Tsokos
articles_hidden.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by pathogenic humoral autoimmunity, yet the mechanisms linking T cell dysfunction to aberrant B cell responses remain poorly defined. Importantly, targeted delivery restored CD8 + T cell function without broad immune perturbation. articles_hidden.title: Leishmania cytochrome bc1 complex inhibition has potential for shortening leishmaniasis treatment duration
articles_hidden.authors: Advait S. Nagle, Yin H. Lai, Diana Caridha, Colin Deniston, Agnes Vidal-Biggart, Lauren C. Davis, Whitney S. Barnes, Casey J. N. Mathison, Mu-Yun Gao, Fang Liang, Xianzhong Liu, Monique Stinson, Jaime Ballard, Vince Yeh, Jeffrey Smith, Xiaodong Liu, Isabelle Lerario, Donatella Chianelli, Yongping Xie, Celine Be, Todd Groessl, Glenn Federe, Jessica Read, Badry Bursulaya, Michael Shapiro, Shilpi Khare, Ansgar Brock, Ben G. Wen, John R. Walker, Tove Tuntland, Srinivas Honnappa, Srinivasa P. S. Rao, Glen Spraggon, Richard J. Glynne, Valentina Molteni, Frantisek Supek
articles_hidden.abstract: Leishmaniasis affects approximately 1 million people annually with visceral infections resulting in death if left untreated and the cutaneous disease leading to disfiguring skin lesions. articles_hidden.title: Isotope evidence for changing methane sources at high northern latitudes
articles_hidden.authors: Xietiancheng Yu, Bibhasvata Dasgupta, Sylvia Englund Michel, John B. Miller, Xin Lan, Sourish Basu, Shinji Morimoto, Ryo Fujita, Daisuke Goto, Thomas Röckmann
articles_hidden.abstract: The renewed increase of methane (CH 4 ) in the atmosphere since 2007 is an imminent threat to the stability of the climate system and undermines climate policy goals. A reversal in the trend of its carbon isotopic composition ( δ 13 C CH4 ) in the 21st century indicates a fundamental shift in the global CH 4 cycle. Here, we investigate the origin of this δ 13 C CH4 trend by determining isotope source signatures of CH 4 emissions based on high and mid-northern latitude observations. A clear latitude gradient and seasonal cycle of the source signatures reflect the spatially and temporally varying contributions of the different sources, each with distinct signatures. We find a large shift in the source signature after 2007 between −3.6 and −5.1‰ at high northern latitudes, and a moderate change between −0.4 and −0.9‰ at mid-northern latitudes. The decrease in δ 13 C CH4 source signature is likely caused by a shift from thermogenic and pyrogenic to microbial sources, accompanied by a likely decrease in the isotopic signature of the microbial emissions, possibly resulting from climate change. Our results suggest that current inverse models may underestimate the shift between fossil and microbial emissions at high northern latitudes, or that microbial methanogenesis pathways change much more strongly than currently believed. Source changes at high latitudes have a disproportionate contribution to the observed trend in atmospheric δ 13 C CH4 .

articles_hidden.title: Microbially driven iron redox chemistry unlocks phosphorus reservoirs in oxygenated soils
articles_hidden.authors: Liping Fang, Jialin Chi, Yanan Ou, Hui Yin, Kai Liu, Yao Yang, Xiangjun Meng, Wenjun Zhang, Xiaoxia Zhou, Christine V. Putnis, Fengchang Wu, Fangbai Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Biological phosphorus (P) mobilization is generally attributed to proton- and ligand-driven dissolution of mineral P, enzymatic hydrolysis of organic P, and, under anoxic conditions, reductive release of phosphate from Fe(III) minerals. Here, we show that extracellular metabolites released by diverse Gram-positive bacteria sustain Fe(III) reduction under oxic conditions, releasing mineral-associated phosphate. The resulting Fe(II) reacts with O 2 to generate reactive oxygen species that activate organic P. This redox pathway was observed across diverse aerobic bacteria and agricultural soils and increased plant-available P. These findings establish aerobic microbial Fe redox chemistry as a previously overlooked route for returning otherwise inaccessible P to bioavailable pools, with implications for reactivating legacy P in agricultural soils.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence for patterns of colonization risk in the nationwide hospitalized patient network in France
articles_hidden.authors: Shrichand Bhuria, Lucille Calmon, Madhav Chaturvedi, Laura Temime, André Karch, Tjibbe Donker, Vittoria Colizza, Pascal Crépey
articles_hidden.abstract: Patient movement within and between hospitals creates a complex hospital network that facilitates the spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria and contributes to healthcare-associated infections. Yet most national-scale studies infer spread from aggregated hospital-to-hospital patient sharing, leaving patient-to-patient contact pathways and the role of routine patient mobility in shaping colonization risk poorly characterized. Using France’s 2023–2024 national hospital-discharge data, we reconstructed a temporal patient-based network of 10.4 million patients across 1,408 acute-care hospitals, comprising 326.6 million overnight ward colocation interactions. We simulated colonization over 365 d on the observed day-by-day temporal network using a stochastic susceptible–colonized–susceptible model, with a mean colonization duration of 180 d. We used national carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) surveillance data to calibrate differences in transmission risk across clinical settings. Across 2,000 simulations initiated on randomly selected dates in 2023, we calculated patient-level colonization probabilities and summarized risk across patients’ residential areas, wards, and hospitals. We further assessed hospital-level consistency between simulated risk and recorded CPE occurrence. Simulated risk was highly heterogeneous across patients and care settings. When mapped by place of residence, hospital-associated colonization risk showed strong spatial clustering in both urban and rural areas. Multivariable regression analyses identified patient- and hospital-level characteristics associated with heterogeneity in simulated colonization risk. Sensitivity analyses varying initial seeding and colonization duration showed that relative risk patterns remained highly stable. This nationwide framework shows how patient mobility and ward colocation patterns can reveal patterns of hospital-associated colonization risk and could support pathogen-specific surveillance and intervention evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: Airborne microbial diversity over Greenlandic and Antarctic plateaus reflects divergent atmospheric connectivity
articles_hidden.authors: Sofía Galbán, Sergi González-Herrero, Marcela Svarc, Pablo Sanz, Ana Justel, Antonio Quesada
articles_hidden.abstract: The polar plateaus are among the most remote environments on Earth. Despite their extreme conditions, these cold deserts on the Greenland and Antarctic Ice Sheets harbor microbial life in snow, ice, and air. However, knowledge of polar airborne microbiomes remains scarce and methodological differences have hindered bipolar comparisons. Here, we present a systematic survey of airborne bacterial and eukaryotic communities across Greenlandic and Antarctic Plateaus, using standardized sampling and genetic techniques, coupled with atmospheric physics and advanced statistical analyses. We found that Antarctic airborne communities are characterized by low diversity and high homogeneity, whereas Greenlandic communities are richer, more variable, and more connected to coastal-marine zones. Our results indicate that atmospheric isolation, together with short-term atmospheric variables, is associated with differences in the microbial biogeography of each Plateau. Compared with Antarctica, the Greenlandic Plateau is more frequently influenced by air masses from outside the plateau over long timescales and exhibits more variable short-term air back-trajectories, reflecting enhanced microbial dispersal and diversity. These findings highlight the potential of polar plateaus as observational platforms for airborne microbial diversity, where sustained and temporally resolved sampling could help assess variations in community composition associated with atmospheric circulation and anthropogenic influence under global change.

articles_hidden.abstract: We describe a severe MEFV -associated autoinflammatory disease, distinct from familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), and designate it CHIVE-18 syndrome (Compound Heterozygosity for I692del and V726A MEFV variants and Elevated IL-18). We present the clinical features and inflammatory signatures of 44 CHIVE-18 patients and 9 other patients with two MEFV variants including I692del. Clinical findings in CHIVE-18 patients often include transfusion-dependent anemia, arthritis, organomegaly, inflammatory bowel disease, failure to thrive, and less frequently cytokine storm, Amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis, and neutrophilic dermatoses. Serum total and free IL-18 levels in CHIVE-18 patients were markedly elevated compared to those of healthy controls, classical FMF patients, and compound heterozygotes for I692del and a pathogenic MEFV variant other than V726A and were comparable to the previously described levels of patients with pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and acne syndrome. Cultured U937 cells expressing the V726A/I692del double mutant exhibited significantly increased release of IL-1β, IL-18, and lactate dehydrogenase compared to the other FMF-associated mutants. Patients’ myeloid cells showed enhanced STAT1 phosphorylation after stimulation with IFNγ. Despite having undetectable serum IL-1β, a previously reported CHIVE-18 patient with autoimmune hepatitis had in situ staining of a liver biopsy that showed high expression of IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-18, which localized to CD68+ tissue macrophages. In summary, CHIVE-18 is a distinct, severe disease that expands the spectrum of MEFV -associated autoinflammatory disorders and highlights genotype/phenotype complexity in compound heterozygous disorders.

articles.title: Rebuilding science’s social contract with the public
articles.abstract: Much has been written about how the social contract between science and society in the United States is in crisis. According to its terms, research will yield broad economic, health, and security benefits to the very public that funds it. But this relationship depends on public trust in science, its systems, and the scientists themselves, and therein lies the problem. Beyond making discoveries and publishing results, scientists shape their own culture, and that is where some changes may be the key to rebuilding public trust.

articles_hidden.title: AI-based digital pathology defines spatial border ecosystems in triple-negative breast cancer
articles_hidden.authors: Hang Zhang, Fan Yang, Pu Tian, Han Wang, Ying Xu, Xiao-Hui Zhu, Xue-Pei Li, Shen Zhao, Yi-Zhou Jiang, Yi Xiao, Zhi-Ming Shao
articles_hidden.abstract: The invasive tumor border in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is currently poorly understood. We integrated digital pathology and spatial multi-omics to define border ecosystems in TNBC. AI-based digital pathology identified five border ecosystems, three associated with prognosis. Spatial multi-omics analyses further resolved the spatial niche, molecular mechanisms and clinical relevance of these ecosystems. Immune-infiltrated borders contain a triadic immune niche associated with favorable prognosis and immunotherapy sensitivity. Tumor–stroma borders harbor a MIF + fibroblast exclusion niche that blocks immune infiltration and suppresses T cells function, predicting poor prognosis. Tumor–adipose borders, featured an FLT1 + endothelial niche, promote hypoxia, vascular leakage, and tumor dissemination. Targeting this niche inhibits tumor progression. Collectively, these findings establish a spatial resource that might enable border-directed therapeutic strategies in TNBC.

articles_hidden.title: Millisecond-scale imaging of fragmented earthquake rupture by near-source fiber-optic sensing
articles_hidden.authors: Sangwoo Han, YoungHee Kim, Jaewoo Kim, Avinash Nayak, Fu Yin, Jonathan Ajo-Franklin
articles_hidden.abstract: Small earthquakes [i.e., those of magnitude ( M ) <3] are commonly modeled as simple circular ruptures, leaving the fine-scale spatial attributes of rupture dynamics unresolved. We used near-source distributed acoustic sensing to image the millisecond-scale rupture of an M 2 earthquake within a swarm sequence in California’s Brawley Seismic Zone. Inverting fiber-derived apparent source time functions revealed two distinct rupture episodes separated by 42 milliseconds, reflecting rupture arrest followed by dynamic renucleation. Analysis of a 3-hour sequence showed adjacent, largely nonoverlapping fault patches activated in succession, forming complementary slip partitioning. These fragmented failure patterns within the M 2 rupture and its sequence limited rupture growth, consistent with the absence of a dominant mainshock. Microearthquakes, which are now accessible by fiber-optic sensing, provide direct constraints on fault mechanics across scales bridging laboratory experiments and large earthquakes.

articles_hidden.title: An engineered cohesion system reduces errors in aged mammalian eggs
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandre Webster, Halima Yusuf, Nina Schweizer, Chloe Charalambous, Eike Urs Mönnich, Heike Eckel, Rüdiger Moltrecht, Martyn Blayney, Kay Elder, Claus Sibold, Andreas Tandler-Schneider, Melina Schuh
articles_hidden.abstract: In humans, female fertility declines rapidly from approximately 35 years onward owing to a steep increase in eggs in which chromosomes have split prematurely or that harbor an incorrect number of chromosomes (aneuploid eggs). A leading cause of age-related aneuploidy in eggs is the premature separation of sister chromatids (PSSC), which is caused by a loss of cohesin from chromosomes. In this study, we created an artificial cohesion system that reduces PSSC in aged mouse eggs. We further engineered a separase-cleavable sequence into the system, allowing for its scheduled deactivation during anaphase. We demonstrated that the artificial cohesion system could be adapted to tether human chromosomes, providing a proof of principle for the future development of approaches to reduce PSSC in eggs from women of advanced reproductive age.

articles_hidden.title: Binding kinetics enable tumor-selective MAPK and growth suppression by a Type 1 RAF inhibitor
articles_hidden.authors: Mathieu Desaunay, Tara L. Peters, Evangelia Matenoglou, Beau Baars, Bijaya Gaire, Ana Orive-Ramos, Li Ren, Joseph P. Lyssikatos, Michael R. Burkard, Dalton Dacus, Matthew J. Sale, Stuart A. Aaronson, Frank McCormick, Evripidis Gavathiotis, Stefan D. Gross, Poulikos I. Poulikakos
articles_hidden.abstract: Targeting the RAS/MAPK pathway has long been constrained by dose-limiting toxicity in normal tissues at doses required for durable tumor control. Although Type 1.5 RAF inhibitors improved selectivity in BRAF(V600X)-monomer tumors, a comparable strategy for RAF dimer-driven cancers, including those with RAS mutations, has been lacking. We describe ELV-3111, a potent Type 1 RAF inhibitor that inhibits RAF dimers and exploits binding kinetics for tumor selectivity. ELV-3111 primes RAF in normal tissues, and its rapid dissociation during drug clearance generates drug-free RAF dimers that paradoxically activate MAPK signaling. RAS-mutant tumors are spared, where RAF is already primed. Combined with a MEK inhibitor, ELV-3111 restored normal tissue signaling while deepening tumor pathway inhibition, producing regressions across RAS- and BRAF-mutant experimental models. Thus, inhibitor dissociation kinetics provide a generalizable source of therapeutic index.
